title: HashMap Architecture: Buckets, Collisions & TreeBins
summary: Deep dive into HashMap: load factor (0.75), initial capacity (16), rehashing, linked list chaining, and Java 8 TreeBin conversion (TREEIFY_THRESHOLD = 8).
prerequisites: The Map Contract: Associative Key-Value Storage
HashSet: How Hash Buckets Guarantee O(1) Lookups
learningObjectives: Master the internal backing array and Node<K,V> bucket architecture of HashMap
Explain load factor (0.75), capacity doubling, and bit-split rehashing without modulo
Trace collision chaining and the Java 8 TreeBin Red-Black tree conversion algorithm
Analyze algorithmic complexity across average O(1) and worst-case O(log N) boundaries
expectedOutcomes: Deep technical mastery of HashMap internals sufficient for elite engineering design interviews
Ability to diagnose and mitigate hash collision attacks and performance bottlenecks

activities.title: Practical Context: Dynamic Warehouse Bin Expansion and Automation

analogy.headline: Practical Context: Dynamic Warehouse Bin Expansion and Automation
analogy.story:
Imagine an automated fulfillment center with 16 storage aisles (buckets). Packages are routed to aisles using the last digits of their tracking code. When an aisle receives multiple packages, warehouse workers stack them sequentially in a single-file line (LinkedList chaining).

If the center reaches 75% total capacity (12 packages), management doubles the warehouse to 32 aisles and re-routes half the packages in each aisle to the newly built aisles. Furthermore, if a single aisle ever accumulates a dangerous bottleneck of 8 packages, robotic stackers convert that specific aisle into an automated multi-level high-density carousel (Red-Black Tree), ensuring packages can still be retrieved in seconds.
analogy.keyTakeaway: HashMap utilizes load factor resizing to spread items across buckets, and converts severely congested chains into Red-Black TreeBins to prevent O(N) degradation.

activities.title: HashMap Architecture: Buckets, Rehashing & Java 8 TreeBins

keyTakeaways: HashMap is backed by a transient Node<K,V>[] table array resized in powers of 2
Default initial capacity is 16; default load factor is 0.75f (resizes at 12 items)
Chains of 8 or more entries convert to Red-Black Trees (TreeBins) if table capacity is at least 64

activities.title: Tracing Bit-Split Rehashing Mechanics
activities.description: Step through a simulation of the exact JDK bit-split rehashing algorithm when expanding from capacity 16 to 32.

steps.description: Define old capacity 16 and new doubled capacity 32 via left shift (oldCap << 1).
Compute old bucket index ((oldCap - 1) & h) and new bucket index ((newCap - 1) & h).
Evaluate the JDK bit test: (h & oldCap) == 0. If 0, the node stays in oldBucket. If non-zero, it moves to oldBucket + 16 directly.

questions.question: What is the threshold for a HashMap bucket chain to convert into a TreeBin in Java 8+?
options: Chain length >= 4, regardless of table capacity
Chain length >= 8 (TREEIFY_THRESHOLD) AND total table capacity >= 64 (MIN_TREEIFY_CAPACITY)
questions.explanation: Java 8 requires two conditions: the bucket must have at least 8 elements, AND the table capacity must be at least 64. If capacity is under 64, it resizes instead.

questions.question: Why does HashMap use (h ^ (h >>> 16)) before masking the bucket index?
options: To spread high-order bits into low-order bits, mitigating poor hash codes that only differ in upper bits
To convert negative integers to positive integers
To compress the object into memory
questions.explanation: Because table capacity is small (e.g., 16), only the lowest 4 bits are used by the mask (n - 1). Shifting high bits down and XORing them ensures high bits influence the bucket choice.

questions.question: What happens when a HashMap reaches its resize threshold (capacity * loadFactor)?
options: It doubles its capacity (2x) and redistributes entries across the new bucket array
questions.explanation: When threshold is reached, HashMap creates a new array of double the capacity (newCap = oldCap << 1) and rehashes entries.

questions.question: When does a TreeBin in a HashMap revert back to a standard linked list (untreeify)?
options: When the tree size shrinks to 6 elements (UNTREEIFY_THRESHOLD)
questions.explanation: To prevent oscillating between tree and list on additions/deletions, untreeification occurs at UNTREEIFY_THRESHOLD = 6, leaving a gap between 6 and 8.

questions.question: Why did Java 8 introduce Red-Black TreeBins into HashMap instead of keeping linked lists?
questions.answer: Prior to Java 8, if malicious actors supplied thousands of keys specifically engineered to produce identical hash codes (a Hash DoS attack), all entries accumulated in a single bucket's linked list. This degraded get() and put() performance from O(1) to O(N), locking up CPU threads and crashing web servers. Java 8 introduced TreeBins so that even under worst-case 100% collision conditions, operations remain strictly bounded at O(log N).

questions.question: Explain how HashMap efficiently redistributes elements during resizing without recalculating hash codes.
questions.answer: Because capacity is always a power of 2, doubling capacity adds exactly one higher-order bit to the mask (n - 1). For example, 16 is mask 01111; 32 is mask 11111. The only bit that changes is bit 4 (value 16). The JDK performs a simple bitwise test: `(e.hash & oldCap) == 0`. If 0, the element stays at its exact old bucket index. If non-zero, it moves to `oldIndex + oldCap`. This requires zero hash calculations and zero expensive modulo operations.

questions.question: What is the optimal initial capacity to set if you know you will store exactly 1,000 items in a HashMap?
questions.answer: To prevent any resizing passes, the capacity must satisfy: `capacity * 0.75 >= 1000`. Dividing 1000 by 0.75 yields approximately 1333.33. Since HashMap capacities must be powers of 2, the next power of 2 above 1334 is 2048 (2^11). Setting `new HashMap<>(2048)` guarantees that all 1,000 items can be inserted with zero rehash passes and optimal bucket distribution.

activities.title: Self-Evaluation: HashMap Architecture
checklist: I can explain the bucket index formula (n - 1) & (h ^ (h >>> 16)) in detail
I understand the conditions for TreeBin conversion (TREEIFY_THRESHOLD = 8 and MIN_TREEIFY_CAPACITY = 64)
I can explain the (hash & oldCap) bit-split algorithm used during capacity doubling

practiceProblems.title: Calculate Exact Bucket Index
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement getBucketIndex(String key, int capacity) using the JDK 8 hash spreading function (h ^ (h >>> 16)) and bitmask (capacity - 1). Handle null keys by returning 0.
hints: Check for key == null first (always bucket 0 in HashMap).

practiceProblems.title: Calculate Optimal Initial Capacity
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Write findOptimalCapacity(int expectedEntries, float loadFactor) that returns the minimum power-of-two capacity required to store expectedEntries without triggering a resize.
hints: Divide expectedEntries by loadFactor and ceil the result.
Find the smallest power of 2 >= that value, with minimum 16.

practiceProblems.title: Simulate Bit-Split Rehash Destination
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Given an integer hash code and oldCapacity of 16, implement willMoveOnResize(int hashCode, int oldCapacity) returning true if the entry moves to oldIndex + 16, or false if it stays.

practiceProblems.title: Verify Treeify Qualification
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement isTreeifyEligible(int chainLength, int tableCapacity) returning true if chainLength >= 8 and tableCapacity >= 64.

practiceProblems.title: Count Collisions in Bucket Array
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Given an array of integer hash codes and a capacity of 16, return the number of buckets that have 2 or more elements mapped to them.
hints: Count how many buckets have counts[i] >= 2.
